name: Guadalajara
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Guadalajara: electronics supplier diligence, nearshoring partners, Jalisco courts and organised crime risk.
hero_lede: Investigative consulting for matters touching Guadalajara, scoped from Nashville: diligence on electronics, software and manufacturing partners in Mexico's main technology cluster, background research for nearshoring investments, and factual support for counsel in disputes before Jalisco's state courts and administrative tribunal.
intro: Guadalajara is the capital of Jalisco and the core of Mexico's third-largest metropolitan area, which had about 5.27 million people across eight municipalities, including Zapopan, Tlaquepaque, Tonalá, Tlajomulco and El Salto, at the 2020 census. Known as Mexico's Silicon Valley, the region is a leading producer of software, electronics and digital components, with facilities of Intel, IBM, Oracle, Jabil, Flex, Sanmina, Siemens, HCL and Tata Consultancy Services. The city accounts for about 37 percent of Jalisco's output, and roughly 40 percent of manufactured products are exported, mostly to the United States. Footwear, textiles, food and beverages remain important, and Expo Guadalajara hosts major trade fairs, including the International Book Fair.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Guadalajara as nearshoring brings new suppliers, landlords and joint venture partners into their supply chains. Electronics and automotive manufacturers need to know who owns contract manufacturers, component distributors and industrial park developers, and whether their history matches their claims. Technology companies hiring through local staffing firms face questions about ownership, labour compliance and intellectual property. Jalisco is also a state where organised crime has penetrated some legitimate business, including real estate, transport and agriculture, so investors and lenders screen counterparties for links to illicit finance. Disputes with municipal and state authorities over permits and procurement add a further layer.

matters.title: Electronics contract manufacturer diligence
matters.text: Researching the ownership, litigation, labour disputes and regulatory record of contract manufacturers, component distributors and service providers in the Guadalajara and Zapopan electronics cluster, so buyers can confirm capability, identify related parties and assess counterfeit, export control and forced labour exposure in supply chains.

matters.title: Nearshoring partner and landlord checks
matters.text: Background research on industrial park developers, landlords, shelter operators and joint venture partners before a plant relocation or expansion, covering shareholders of record, related companies, property disputes and permit history in municipalities such as El Salto and Tlajomulco.

matters.title: Organised crime and illicit finance screening
matters.text: Screening counterparties in real estate, transport, agriculture and hospitality for documented links to organised crime or money laundering, using judgments, official announcements, sanctions lists and Spanish-language media, so clients can make proportionate decisions and avoid entering relationships that create criminal or regulatory exposure.

matters.title: Technology staffing and IP concerns
matters.text: Researching staffing firms, software contractors and former employees in suspected leaks of code, designs or customer data, identifying related companies and new employers through public records, and supporting counsel in assessing claims under Mexican law without covert or unlawful methods.

matters.title: Municipal and state procurement review
matters.text: Researching suppliers and contractors that win work from Jalisco and metropolitan municipal governments, including their owners, links to officials and history before the state administrative tribunal, to identify conflicts of interest and corruption risks before clients partner with or acquire them.

local_context.title: Jalisco state judiciary
local_context.text: Commercial and civil disputes involving Guadalajara companies are heard largely by the Jalisco state judiciary, whose Organic Law establishes the Supremo Tribunal de Justicia, first-instance and specialised courts, and the Consejo de la Judicatura as its administrative body. Most commercial litigation in the metropolitan area is filed in Guadalajara, and Mexican federal courts also hear commercial matters, so searches must cover both state and federal dockets.

local_context.title: Alternative justice institute
local_context.text: The same Organic Law recognises the Instituto de Justicia Alternativa del Estado de Jalisco, governed by the state's Alternative Justice Law, which provides mediation and conciliation services. Agreements reached through it can carry legal effect, so a counterparty's dispute history may include settled matters that never reached court. Commercial arbitration in Guadalajara is generally administered privately and is confidential, so awards rarely appear in public sources.

local_context.title: State administrative tribunal
local_context.text: The Tribunal de Justicia Administrativa del Estado de Jalisco, headquartered in Guadalajara, resolves disputes between private parties and state and municipal authorities and sanctions serious administrative misconduct by public servants and the private parties involved. It received 28,663 claims in 2024, the most of any Mexican state administrative tribunal, and more than half are now filed online. Its decisions are a useful record of permit, tax and procurement disputes.

local_context.title: Jalisco anti-corruption system
local_context.text: Jalisco operates a State Anti-Corruption System (SEAJAL) alongside the national system, with a state anti-corruption policy that public bodies, including the administrative tribunal, are adopting with targets to 2030. Serious misconduct cases involving companies that contract with the state can lead to sanctions on those companies, which makes the tribunal's records and state announcements directly relevant to counterparty diligence on government suppliers.

local_context.title: Export manufacturing framework
local_context.text: Jalisco has more than 280 establishments under Mexico's IMMEX export manufacturing programme, employing over 130,000 people, and has ranked among the leading states for new foreign direct investment. Companies operating under IMMEX carry customs obligations for temporarily imported goods, so diligence on a contract manufacturer often covers whether its programme status, customs record and inventory controls are in order.

tdsc_approach: For matters touching Guadalajara, TDSC begins by identifying the decision at stake, whether that is selecting a contract manufacturer, signing a lease in an industrial park or entering a joint venture, and the records that bear on it: commercial registry entries, Jalisco and federal court dockets, administrative tribunal decisions, IMMEX status and Spanish-language media. Research is conducted from Nashville. Where site visits, registry retrieval or interviews are needed, TDSC coordinates with qualified local professionals and the client's Mexican counsel. Organised crime screening is handled carefully, without contact with the subjects, and findings state the evidence behind them. Personal data is handled in line with Mexican data protection law.

faqs.q: How do you check a contract manufacturer in Guadalajara?
faqs.a: We confirm the company's registration, shareholders and legal representatives, then search state and federal court records, administrative tribunal decisions, labour disputes and media. We compare what we find with the supplier's claims about capacity, customers and certifications, and flag related companies or common owners that suggest the supplier may not be what it appears.

faqs.q: Can you screen Jalisco counterparties for organised crime links?
faqs.a: Yes, through lawful sources: sanctions lists, published judgments, official announcements and credible investigative reporting. We report documented links and their sources and distinguish them from rumour. We do not contact subjects or use covert methods, and where findings raise safety or criminal law concerns we advise the client to involve counsel promptly.

faqs.q: Which courts should we search for a Guadalajara company's disputes?
faqs.a: Commercial claims may be heard by Jalisco state courts or by federal courts, and disputes with authorities by the state administrative tribunal. Mediated settlements through the Instituto de Justicia Alternativa and private arbitrations may not appear at all. We search the public sources available and state clearly where gaps remain.

faqs.q: Do nearshoring investments in Guadalajara need special diligence?
faqs.a: Rapid growth in industrial parks and supplier networks means new counterparties with short track records. We look at who owns the land, developer and shelter operator, whether permits and title have been disputed, and whether partners have links to officials or to businesses that create reputational or legal risk.

faqs.q: Does TDSC have an office in Guadalajara?
faqs.a: No. TDSC is based in Nashville and has no office or staff in Guadalajara or elsewhere in Mexico. Most of our work is desk-based research in Spanish and English. Where on-the-ground steps are needed, we coordinate with qualified local professionals acting lawfully and with the client's Mexican counsel.
